The answer will most likely be working for the maximum of the assignment. If you have your aim low you might give up before you achieve a task even if that was an important task. If your aim is high you won't give up and achieve the task. Therefore, having your aim higher is better than just trying to do the easiest thing you can.

Some people might say that by setting the aim too high that can make them suffer. This can be true, but that does not mean you should aim too low. what is important is to keep everything balanced to the best. Everyone has been said to eat a balanced meal when they were a small child. This is the same for everything. Understanding your own abilities and setting the aim to what you can possibly achieve rather than setting the goal for something easy. Some might say that if people don't aim high they won't have to work hard, so they will have less stress. They might have less stress but not every stress is bad for people. Stress can even help people sometimes. For example, I was a student in Japan that hated school and was too lazy to do any work. I had a lot of stress and that made me stay at home all the time. Staying at home did not relieve my stress at all, and I did not feel good about my self. Therefore, I chose to go to school again. Stress will mostly affect bad for you, but there are good affects too.

Finally, The hole point about this is that running away and choosing the easy way is not the best decision. Aiming low might look like it's the simple and easy way thats safer but whats really the danger is for people to forget to aim high and believe they can achieve great things. The best is to make a decision that wont make you regret and making the best aim you can make. No one has to be excellent or perfect, but everyone should try their best in their short life so they can die with no regret.

Query: ## Essay:
"Studies have shown that one way to improve student achievement is to start an after school homework club." Two-thirds of the students who join an after school activity club are more likely to succeed in academics then students who do not. Schools should establish an after school homework club because it can help students finish their homework, become more socially interactive , and give students some teaching experience.

Firstly, an after school homework club helps students finish their homework in time. Many student get a low grade in their class because of unfinished homework. They were not able to finish their homework because, they did not know how to do it. Teachers do not usually have the time to go through each student, and help them in class, but some teachers volunteer to meet with students who have difficulty in certain subjects in an after school homework club. Joining an after school homework club is a great way to finish your homework in time. Sometimes teacher might even give students some tips and tricks on how to solve a question, that they would not give out in class. My friend Generic_Name used to have a lot of difficulties with his math homework until he joined the after school homework club in our school. He learned many tricks on how to solve a math equation and even taught a trick to solve an "Integer Slope Inequality" equation.

Moving on, an after school homework club can help students become more socially interactive. While in an after school homework club, you can find students with the same difficulties as you. This will give students something to relate to and not feel out of place. Having group discussions on how to solve a problem and having group projects in your club will also help you be more socially interactive. My friend Generic_Name made many friends by joining the after school homework club in our school, and grew a lot of confidence. He is now much less nervous when talking to people than before.

Lastly, homework clubs can give students teaching experience for if they want to be a teacher when they grow up. Students can volunteer to help other students finish their homework in an after school homework club. This will give the student a lot of experience on how to teach, and deal with other students. There is a team of students is our school called the " Junior Honor Society", which helps students with academic difficulties every day after school. As a member, I have learned about a lot of ways to teach someone else, and because of my desire to be a teacher one day, this helps me a lot.

Schools should establish homework clubs because it can help students finish their homework, become more socially interactive , and can give students teaching experience. Ten out ten students have said that, joining an after school homework club has been the best decision they made in their life.

Require the judge to cite exact phrases or clauses that support cohesion, syntax, etc., and to quote minimal text fragments (1–2 words or a short clause) as anchor points. This makes ratings traceable and reproducible.

- Tie rubric to concrete features: For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), specify concrete criteria aligned with typical grades for high-school essays. For example:
  - Cohesion: track throughline, transitions, logical flow between paragraphs, use of connectors, topic progression.
  - Syntax: variety of sentence types, sentence length balance, avoidance of run-ons/splice errors.
  - Vocabulary: precision, range, appropriateness to audience, avoidance of overgeneralization.
  - Phraseology: idiom use, collocations, natural phrasing, lexical bundles, and meter of prose.
  - Grammar: subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, pronoun references.
  - Conventions: spelling, capitalization, punctuation, paragraphing, title conventions, quotation marks.

- Add a two-tier evidence system: For each attribute, require:
  - Primary justification: a concise statement linking to a specific rubric criterion.
  - Secondary evidence: one or two sentence-level examples from the essay (with short quotes) illustrating the point. If quotes are unavailable, paraphrase closely with page/line-like references.

- Calibrate severity with context: Explicitly acknowledge the target audience (English language learners in grades 8–12) and allow for acceptable deviations from native-like perfection. Include a rule like: minor punctuation or occasional run-on sentences may not drastically reduce readability for this level, while persistent structural flaws should.

- Avoid blanket granularity traps: Replace generic phrases like “the text struggles with coherence” with granular observations such as:
  - “Paragraph 2 shifts topic abruptly without a transitional sentence.”
  - “A comma splice joins two independent clauses in the sentence ‘X, Y’ which affects readability.”
  - “There is evidence of repetition without advancing the argument, e.g., repeated motif ‘control’ without new insight.”

- Require error severity weighting: When a rating diverges from human judgment, specify how much weight is given to each sub-criterion and explain the human-consensus expectation. For example, if cohesion is weak due to abrupt transitions, assign higher weight to cohesion rather than syntax unless the syntax errors are severe.

- Encourage a balanced assessment: The prompt should prompt the judge to acknowledge strengths (e.g., clear thesis about personal responsibility, use of quotations) and explain how these justify higher scores in certain attributes, rather than only listing flaws.

- Provide a calibration note template: End with a concise calibration statement that links observed evidence to rubric scores, such as:
  - “Cohesion: human readers note a throughline about self-control; transitions are imperfect but present. If rubrics allow, score 3–4 with justification citing connectors or repeated themes.”
  - “Conventions: several spelling and punctuation slips, but no pervasive errors; adjust toward 3 with examples.”

- Ensure traceability and reproducibility: The system prompt should instruct the judge to produce a per-attribute justification block (even if the final output is a single numeric line). This helps downstream users audit, adjust, and calibrate the evaluator.

- Improve language for calibration: Replace absolute, blanket statements with measured phrasing that accounts for context, e.g., “The evidence suggests some alignment with the criterion, though signs of overgeneralization reduce reliability of the rating,” instead of “The rating is too low.”

- Define how to handle quotations: If the text includes quotations, specify how to evaluate quotation accuracy, integration with the argument, and whether quotation use supports cohesion and stance.

- Add a reliability check: Include a brief, mandatory self-check step: “If any rubric criterion cannot be clearly evidenced in the text, mark the criterion as N/A and justify why.” This prevents overstating issues that aren’t observable.

  - Evidence present? Yes/No
  - Example sentence(s) cited? Yes/No
  - Alignment with rubric weight? High/Medium/Low
  - Suggested adjustment to rating range? (e.g., raise 1–2 points if throughline exists but transitions weak)

- Language and formatting: Recommend bulleted, per-attribute rubrics with parallel structure to ease parsing by an automated system. This increases consistency across evaluations and improves interoperability with the broader optimization task.

- coherence: Evaluate how much the story makes sense. Rate from 1 to 5.
- empathy: Evaluate how well you understood the characters' emotions. Rate from 1 to 5.

Query: ## Writing prompt:
A warrior from a planetary culture with literally no concept of surrender or quarter sits detained in a POW camp.

## Story:
Jackson had been a soldier in the 15 years war of China back in 2225, and he had seen atrocities. Atrocities was a good word for his experiences there, he felt. Short, and simple. He liked that, because it made a hellish nightmare easy to grasp in his mind. He had seen atrocities. When he returned to the Fractured States after the American, and West European victory over China, job opportunities were scarce, to put it in simple terms. The war had damaged Jackson in a fundamental way. Physically, he was fine. He had come back unharmed, save a few small scars he 'd picked up sharpening his Bowie knife. His mind though, had been fractured worse than the United States had been when the Chinese launched the unexpected nuclear missiles that began the 15 Years War of China. When a man in a fine suit came, and offered him a job as a guard in a mining camp on a far off planet he could hardly refuse. Not because the pay was good, it was, but because life on Earth was frightening. He 'd seen what men could do to each other, and that fear would never leave, no matter where he went on Earth. The fine suited man offered him a job on that lush green planet that sat almost cozily on the boarder of the Milky Way. The life provided there offered him a feeling of security, and safety he had not felt in months since returning home. On this planet he could have a sense of security knowing that the total population was roughly 500 humans, mining the planet 's metal resources, and security staff guarding the miners from the planet 's local inhabitants. With a population like that there was n't a chance of mass war extinction. Jackson had never left the Earth 's lovely, life giving atmosphere before so the experience of leaving on a rocket was thrilling for him, and even, oddly enough, made him relax for the duration of the ride to his new home for the next decade. Leaving the planet he was born on had been an experience that he did n't expect to be topped, at least not soon. What he found on his new home shattered his previous exhilaration. Jackson had been on his new planet one week. One week to learn the layout of the bases, mine locations, and being briefed on the local life forms. At the end of that first week, he was introduced to the specimen research facility located 35 miles from where he landed, and another 43 miles further away from the mining operations. That was where he encountered the *thing* that would bring him a new thrill. It sat in a cell with steel bars across the front that were thicker than Jackson 's torso was. It sat with its arms pulled behind its back cuffed at the wrists, what Jackson presumed would be its elbows, and finally a chain around its neck that wrapped the upper portion of its arms. It was shockingly human in its general body structure. Single head, a torso with two arms that looked almost cartoonishly muscular, as were the neck and chest of this creature. The arms were long like a gorilla 's and it had short, stocky legs. It did n't look like a runner. It stood ramrod straight as soon as Jackson entered the cell hall and saw him. The human symmetry was were the similarities ended though. While humans were anywhere from a pale white to a dark brown this thing was red, almost like a fruit with patterns that changed shades of red all over its body. “That there mother is our prized specimen ,” began Captain Cage, Jackson 's supervisor. Captain Cage continued “We have him chained like that because when we first brought him in he broke the original chains we had on him and damn near broke out his cell. He mangled one of our recruits that got too close to the cell bars while he was rampaging. After that little display we thickened his cell bars, and gave him extra chains, courtesy of upper management .” Jackson responded with a simple murmur. He was n't much for talk. “I call him Rattles ,” Captain Cage said, almost affectionately. “He likes to become active at night and rattle in his cell, and keep us all up at night .” Silence fell over the two men as they observed Rattles, and Rattles in turn observed them. Jackson had taken a disliking to Rattles within seconds of seeing it when he walked in, and after another moment of silent observation he realized why. “Rattles is intelligent, is n't he ?” Jackson marveled. “More than intelligent. He 's god damned cunning. After we upped his security he spent four days just laying in a corner ignoring his food. We thought he had expired in captivity, but when we sent guys in to collect the specimen, the moment he heard the lock click he jumped up, and flayed Anderson 's arm. Thankfully we had multiple locks on the cell door, so Anderson was the only casualty .” Captain Cage explained. after

Improve by embedding concrete criteria for each dimension (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions) that map directly to the essay’s visible elements (thesis, argument structure, transitions, tense consistency, word choice appropriate for ESL level).

Include prompts to assess premise-support patterns, presence of a thesis, and consideration of counterarguments, with scoring cues tied to these features.

Provide examples of when tone shifts undermine persuasiveness, and specify how to rate those disruptions.

This anchors the evaluation and reduces generic feedback.

- Include a diagnostic checklist and quick diagnostic prompts: Add a short, standardized set of checks such as:
  - Thesis presence: “Identify the main claim about electives vs required arts.”
  - Premises: “List two supporting reasons given.”
  - Counterpoints: “Is a counterargument acknowledged or addressed?”
  - Transitions: “Are there bridging phrases between ideas?”
  - Evidence of cohesion: “Do repeated terms (electives, arts, motivation) anchor the article?”
  - Grammatical accuracy: “Note recurring errors (subject-verb agreement, tense shifts).”
  - Conventions: “Punctuation, capitalization, quotation marks usage.”
  This enables consistent, repeatable scoring.

- Emphasize diagnostic, not prescriptive, feedback: Reframe judgments as observations about the text and potential improvements rather than definitive fixes. Use phrases like “the text would benefit from,” “this pattern suggests,” or “to strengthen cohesion, consider…” without prescribing a fixed rewrite.

- Provide weightings that reflect scholarly ESL evaluation: Recommend weights that reflect instructionally meaningful priorities for a high school ESL persuasive essay, e.g., give more weight to cohesion and argument structure than to minor grammar surface issues, since readers attend to overall coherence before micro-issues.

- Clarify handling of non-native errors: Distinguish between general-ESL features (article usage, prepositions, verb tense consistency) and more universal writing flaws (logical fallacies, unsupported claims). Instruct the judge to annotate both observable surface issues and underlying coherence problems, with separate rubric notes.

- Ensure operable prompts and output structure: Redesign the system prompt to require: (a) explicit mapping per rubric to textual evidence, (b) a concise justification statement for each score, and (c) a final, rubric-aligned overall recommendation. This makes outputs more actionable for optimization.

- Include failure-mode safeguards: Add reminders to avoid over-claiming about author intent, to not rely on assumed external knowledge, and to flag ambiguous passages where the judgment would be speculative.

- Encourage consistency and auditability: Add a requirement to note any deviations from typical ESL curricula expectations, and to record any uncertainties with a lower confidence tag, enabling better aggregation across samples.

- Prevent overly harsh or unjustified judgments: Incorporate tone and politeness guidelines so the judge remains constructive, especially when rating content from an English learner.

- Accessibility for future samples: Write the prompt to generalize beyond a single essay prompt, enabling robust evaluation of varied student writing topics while preserving the rubric’s interpretability.

  This keeps feedback granular, observable, and actionable.

- Avoid conflating surface errors with meaning: The prompt should separate surface conventions (spelling/punctuation) from deeper coherence and argumentation, ensuring that a text with minor orthographic slips isn’t downgraded unduly if its argument is otherwise strong.

- Embed an example-annotated rubric template: Provide a ready-to-use structure where each rubric line includes: dimension, observed issue, impact on evaluation, and recommended diagnostic action. This facilitates fast, consistent scoring across samples.

- Preserve a clear hierarchy of performance levels: Ensure the rubric defines what constitutes 1, 3, or 5 in a way that reflects both linguistic accuracy and argumentative clarity, so evaluators can justify scores with aligned textual evidence.

The life provided there offered him a feeling of security, and safety he had not felt in months since returning home. On this planet he could have a sense of security knowing that the total population was roughly 500 humans, mining the planet 's metal resources, and security staff guarding the miners from the planet 's local inhabitants. With a population like that there was n't a chance of mass war extinction. Jackson had never left the Earth 's lovely, life giving atmosphere before so the experience of leaving on a rocket was thrilling for him, and even, oddly enough, made him relax for the duration of the ride to his new home for the next decade. Leaving the planet he was born on had been an experience that he did n't expect to be topped, at least not soon. What he found on his new home shattered his previous exhilaration. Jackson had been on his new planet one week. One week to learn the layout of the bases, mine locations, and being briefed on the local life forms. At the end of that first week, he was introduced to the specimen research facility located 35 miles from where he landed, and another 43 miles further away from the mining operations. That was where he encountered the *thing* that would bring him a new thrill. It sat in a cell with steel bars across the front that were thicker than Jackson 's torso was. It sat with its arms pulled behind its back cuffed at the wrists, what Jackson presumed would be its elbows, and finally a chain around its neck that wrapped the upper portion of its arms. It was shockingly human in its general body structure. Single head, a torso with two arms that looked almost cartoonishly muscular, as were the neck and chest of this creature. The arms were long like a gorilla 's and it had short, stocky legs. It did n't look like a runner. It stood ramrod straight as soon as Jackson entered the cell hall and saw him. The human symmetry was were the similarities ended though. While humans were anywhere from a pale white to a dark brown this thing was red, almost like a fruit with patterns that changed shades of red all over its body. “That there mother is our prized specimen ,” began Captain Cage, Jackson 's supervisor. Captain Cage continued “We have him chained like that because when we first brought him in he broke the original chains we had on him and damn near broke out his cell. He mangled one of our recruits that got too close to the cell bars while he was rampaging. After that little display we thickened his cell bars, and gave him extra chains, courtesy of upper management .” Jackson responded with a simple murmur. He was n't much for talk. “I call him Rattles ,” Captain Cage said, almost affectionately. “He likes to become active at night and rattle in his cell, and keep us all up at night .” Silence fell over the two men as they observed Rattles, and Rattles in turn observed them. Jackson had taken a disliking to Rattles within seconds of seeing it when he walked in, and after another moment of silent observation he realized why. “Rattles is intelligent, is n't he ?” Jackson marveled. “More than intelligent. He 's god damned cunning. After we upped his security he spent four days just laying in a corner ignoring his food. We thought he had expired in captivity, but when we sent guys in to collect the specimen, the moment he heard the lock click he jumped up, and flayed Anderson 's arm. ## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.

  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.

  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

  - For each attribute, map observed features directly to rubric anchors (cohesion: thesis presence, transitions; syntax: sentence variety; vocabulary: precision; phraseology: idiomatic usage; grammar: agreement/tense; conventions: spelling/punctuation).
  - Add explicit recoverability notes (e.g., “Adding a clear thesis sentence and transitional connectors would raise cohesion from 3 to 4/5.”).

- Acknowledge strengths and calibrate upward when justified
  - Extend the prompt to identify constructive strengths (e.g., “three-key framework aids cohesion”) and require the evaluator to adjust the score when the student demonstrates a coherent albeit imperfect structure. Encourage arguing for partial credit where strengths exist.

- Diagnose and surface overlooked pitfalls
  - Instruct the evaluator to flag recurring capitalization issues, article misuse, inconsistent pluralization, tense shifts, and punctuation problems, with explicit citations from the essay.
  - Add a clause to explicitly assess and report on surface vs. discourse-level issues, so conventions and grammar are not conflated.

- Strengthen evaluator reasoning with exemplar references
  - Require the evaluator to quote or paraphrase representative lines illustrating each critique (e.g., a sentence that breaks parallelism or a misplaced modifier). Tie each exemplar to the corresponding rating.

- Enhance procedural coherence for each attribute
  - Structure the evaluation as: for each attribute, present (a) Observation (quote + locator), (b) Issue identified (concise label), (c) Evidence-linked justification (why this affects the score), (d) Suggested fix (concrete action), (e) Impact on score (if fixed, how much the score could improve).

- Specify output formatting and consistency
  - Ensure the evaluation outputs a compact, criterion-by-criterion critique, not a single generic sentence. Each attribute should have a short paragraph with bullet-like clarity but remain within the single JSON line requirement eventually (the JSON line could embed compact subfields or a standardized compact rubric-coded string, but maintain interpretability).

- Expand calibration rules and bias awareness
  - Add a note about potential biases: ESL texts may have systematic resource-access gaps (e.g., limited vocabulary, article usage). Instruct the evaluator to separate language learnability from overall quality and to adjust the scoring scale accordingly (e.g., allow 0.5 increments to reflect near-misses).

- Provide actionable improvement steps per attribute
  - For cohesion: specify where to insert transition markers (e.g., “First,” “Second,” “Lastly”), and suggest ensuring a clear thesis statement in the opening paragraph.
  - For syntax: recommend varying sentence length, combining short sentences with complex ones, and ensuring proper boundaries.
  - For vocabulary: flag repeated high-use terms and propose synonyms or paraphrase opportunities.
  - For phraseology: call out awkward collocations and propose native-like alternatives, with examples.
  - For grammar: target subject-verb agreement and tense consistency with concrete corrections (e.g., “is” vs. “are” with plural subjects, or consistent past tense for narrative).
  - For conventions: highlight capitalization of proper nouns and the essay’s opening sentence, punctuation like commas before coordinating conjunctions, and paragraphing clarity.

- Implement a confidence and reliability note
  - Add a brief reliability statement per evaluation to indicate uncertainty level (e.g., “score based on 90% of observable text; remaining sections would refine scores with more data”).

- Encourage dynamic, exemplar-based scoring
  - When possible, the evaluator should present two contrasting examples: one showing a near-satisfactory attribute with minor fixes, and one showing a major flaw requiring structural revision. This clarifies what “recoverability” looks like in practice.

- Practical phrasing refinements for the system prompt
  - Replace vague terms like “basic argument” with precise rubric-linked language (e.g., “present thesis and three supporting points; transitions inadequately bridge paragraphs”).
  - Include explicit instructions to avoid generic praise/criticism and to favor evidence-based, testable claims about the text.

- Example of a strengthened directive (conceptual)
  - For each attribute: “Identify the thesis presence and transitions; quote sentences that show transitions or lack thereof; count x fragmentation issues; assign a score and justify with precise references; propose y concrete edits and describe the expected improvement in score.”

Overall objective: Transform the system prompt into a rigorously rubric-aligned, evidence-driven evaluator that produces precise, actionable feedback with explicit textual references, measurable diagnostics, and clear improvement pathways. This will directly support the <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> by yielding granular, justifiable, and actionable scoring that ESL learners can use to improve.

## Task
Evaluate the Story, written in response to the Writing prompt, using the Instructions below.
1. Consider every strength and flaw you find when making your evaluation.
2. Based on the number and severity of the strengths and flaws, assign a value.

## Instructions:
- relevance: Evaluate how well the story matches its writing prompt. Rate from 1 to 5.
- coherence: Evaluate how much the story makes sense. Rate from 1 to 5.
- empathy: Evaluate how well you understood the characters' emotions. Rate from 1 to 5.
- surprise: Evaluate how surprising the end of the story is. Rate from 1 to 5.
- engagement: Evaluate how much you engaged with the story. Rate from 1 to 5.
- complexity: Evaluate how elaborate the story is. Rate from 1 to 5.
Query: ## Writing prompt:
Write a rearrangeable story. Write two or more paragraphs that can be read in any order to form a unique, coherent story.

## Story:
Dave adjusted his light headpiece. The full moon shone across the ceiling on a humid January morning. The air was almost suffocating. He sighed, relieved he hadn't left his apartment alone at 10:00 AM. His day started with his childhood toy car. He drove it home before it got towed. He spent many hours in it. He even bought a couple of cables for it. He couldn’t do much with those nowadays, but he enjoyed watching television. Dave switched on the television on, staring at the bright show. His eye widened. The number 666 on the screen began to read. Dave sighed. What if he could just turn on that. He stuck his thumb into his pocket and pulled out a plastic box. He took out a few coins and slid them into the cardboard box. He cracked open the box and put one coin into his hand. The lights flickered on and off. Dave smiled as he opened the box. Dave sat on a gurney, looking out at the sea. He never really thought about the dreams that he had, but he was always dreaming of them. Maybe tomorrow morning he would wake up and make something happen. Tomorrow he would go out and buy groceries. He still knew that he needed to act to help people who needed it. But tomorrow he was going to get married. He had to act and make a name for himself. “Hello, Dave,” A beautiful woman said from the kitchen. “Who are you?” Dave inquired. “I am your manager, Marie,” Marie replied. “Ahh, Dave. What’s going on? I think you have a bit of a headache,” Dave said with a frown. “What the hell is going on?” “We’re actually only talking about your wife, Marie. Her name is Sarah. Sarah and I were taking you to Disneyland for a Christmas dinner. We came up with the idea that we would drive around the world and get some of the big attractions of this year.” “

  - Ground assessments in concrete evidence: For each rating (syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), quote or paraphrase specific issues from the essay (e.g., misused verb forms, repeated simple words, paragraph breaks, capitalization errors). This makes the feedback actionable.
  - Distinguish between surface-level and deeper issues: Separate observations about mechanical errors (syntax/grammar/conventions) from stylistic and argumentative aspects (phraseology, cohesion). The essay’s attempt at balance should be weighed against the explicit criteria the human raters used.
  - Calibrate strength of claims to consistency with human ratings: If humans rate cohesion at 2.5 and the essay shows episodic flow, acknowledge partial alignment and specify where the flow breaks (e.g., abrupt topic shifts, missing transitions). Avoid blanket statements like “overall weakness” without mapping to sections.
  - Increase specificity in syntax and grammar critiques: Move beyond “vague issues” to pinpoint patterns (e.g., subject-verb agreement errors, noun-pronoun consistency, tense management). Provide short, concrete revision hints (e.g., “correct: ‘this technology is’ vs. ‘the technology is’”).
  - Refine vocabulary and phraseology analysis: Note where vocabulary is basic yet effective (e.g., accurate use of “maps,” “online banking”) and where repetitiveness or nonstandard collocations appear. Suggest categories of improvement: register, collocations, and evaluative tone (e.g., balancing positive/negative claims).
  - Improve evaluative pedagogy: Instead of a binary or generic verdict, present a tiered rubric mapping to the 1–5 scale with justifications: e.g., syntax errors that impede readability vs. stylistic choices that still convey meaning; the presence of stance signals in phrases like “positive because…”
  - Propose concrete, text-referenced revision directions: For each dimension, offer 2–3 actionable revise-and-test steps such as “replace repeated ‘you need to’ with varied constructions,” “add transitional phrases to improve cohesion between ideas about benefits and drawbacks,” or “correct capitalization and punctuation to retain professional tone.”
  - Address potential bias in evaluation: The judge should explicitly acknowledge any over- or under-weighting of certain issues (e.g., overemphasis on grammar while missing stance cues) and correct this by cross-checking with the human rubric.

- Specific feedback lines to incorporate for the given span:
  - Syntax: Identify a few sentences where word order or verb tense disrupts comprehension; suggest rewriting variants that preserve meaning but fix tense consistency (e.g., “This technology can help you…”) and propose noting recurring syntactic patterns to target systematically.
  - Vocabulary: Call out instances of basic lexis that are effective versus repeated simple terms that reduce perceived sophistication; recommend varying lexis through synonyms and domain-specific terms (e.g., “navigation apps,” “e-commerce,” “accessibility”).
  - Phraseology: Point out places where evaluative stance could be signaled more clearly (e.g., “I think technology is good because…” vs. weaker phrases); encourage highlighting explicit balance with nuanced qualifiers.
  - Grammar: Track consistent errors (subject-verb agreement, article usage, pluralization) and suggest marking a handful of representative errors with targeted correction rules.
  - Conventions: Flag capitalization, punctuation, and paragraphing issues with explicit examples from the text; propose guidelines for capitalization of “I,” start-of-sentence punctuation, and paragraph segmentation to improve readability.

- Overall methodological improvement:
  - Adopt a minimal, reproducible rubric: For each attribute, provide 1–2 specific, checkable criteria tied to the essay, followed by precise corrective suggestions.
  - Ensure output traces back to the human ratings: When the judge claims alignment or misalignment, attach direct references to the corresponding human scores and examples from the essay to justify the stance.

- End-user benefit: With these changes, the judge’s feedback becomes diagnostic and actionable, enabling the optimizer to adjust the variable to produce clearer, better-targeted evaluations that align more closely with human judgments.

Dave adjusted his light headpiece. The full moon shone across the ceiling on a humid January morning. The air was almost suffocating. He sighed, relieved he hadn't left his apartment alone at 10:00 AM. His day started with his childhood toy car. He drove it home before it got towed. He spent many hours in it. He even bought a couple of cables for it. He couldn’t do much with those nowadays, but he enjoyed watching television. Dave switched on the television on, staring at the bright show. His eye widened. The number 666 on the screen began to read. Dave sighed. What if he could just turn on that. He stuck his thumb into his pocket and pulled out a plastic box. He took out a few coins and slid them into the cardboard box. He cracked open the box and put one coin into his hand. The lights flickered on and off. Dave smiled as he opened the box. Dave sat on a gurney, looking out at the sea. He never really thought about the dreams that he had, but he was always dreaming of them. Maybe tomorrow morning he would wake up and make something happen. Tomorrow he would go out and buy groceries. He still knew that he needed to act to help people who needed it. But tomorrow he was going to get married. He had to act and make a name for himself. “Hello, Dave,” A beautiful woman said from the kitchen. “Who are you?” Dave inquired. “I am your manager, Marie,” Marie replied. “Ahh, Dave. What’s going on? I think you have a bit of a headache,” Dave said with a frown. “What the hell is going on?” “We’re actually only talking about your wife, Marie. Her name is Sarah. Introduce a lightweight taxonomy of evidence types (e.g., lexical choice, syntactic pattern, discourse marker presence). System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.

People that have their faces in front of a screen with there back slouching with the help of technology. Technology is advancing year by year and month by month. When teens or adults get there hands on the new technology they will spend weeks or even months in their rooms, trying to figure out what the device can and cannot do. The limitation of human contact due to the use of technology has a negative effect on peoples lives, because it can lead to bad communication skills, health problems and being inactive.

However, not everyone agrees with this statement. Some people claim that technology has a positive effect on peoples lives. Neverless, this position overlooks an important point, mainly that technology cannot change how much human contact you have or do not have. For example, my friend she cannot drive, but she can have items get delivered to her; books, food, and clothes. Furthermore, when the delivery person came she did not know the proper way to greet him. Do to technology, people can have bad communication skills and they don't know how to communicate with people when they are in contact with someone.

Moreover, by being isolated, technology can lead to bad communication skills. When someone gets the newest device or game, they want to know how it works. By learning what the device or video game can and cannot do, they usually spend a month learning how the device works or how to unlock the next level in the game. For instance, my brother got a new video game, he has isolated himself in his room, so he can beat the level and go on to the next. When he was finish with the level, he had a hard time communicating properly. Before he played his video game, his grammar was good; now it wasn't. For example he would use the wrong past and present tense. Thus, by staring at the screen for so long, he has got very inactive.

Additionally, sitting on the couch or in a chair with a screen in front of you, every day for a whole month can make a person inactive. People that are inactive can become very lazy, and they intend on making a lot of mistakes when they are talking. They can also gain weight or have health problems. To illustrate, sitting in front of a screen while eating junk food can cause you to gain weight and can lead to health issues. During spring break, my friend had nothing to do, he was on his laptop everyday eating junk food.

Now he has to be careful on what he can and cannot eat, because he will get heart burn.

If he does not stop eating unhealthy foods in front of a screen he will gain more weight and have more health issues.

He does not know how to ask for help; he needs someone to push him to go outside and enjoy the weather, instead of being in front of a screen all day long.

Based on this argument, one must conclude that the limitation of human contact due to the use of technology has a negative effect on peoples lives. Technology can effect us in many different ways; bad communication skills, health problems and being inactive. In conclusion, technology can change human contact in a negative way.

- Align the system prompt with explicit, criterion-driven calibration: The current prompt overpromises objectivity but then accepts broad, value-laden judgments. Strengthen the rubric anchoring by requiring the judge to map each observed feature directly to the defined scale (1–5) with explicit ranges tied to rubric anchors (e.g., cohesion: 1 = minimal progression; 5 = clear thesis with logical sequencing). This reduces variance and makes recoverability guidance more actionable.

- Make evidence-first evaluation explicit: Require the judge to quote or paraphrase exact sentences as evidence for every claim, and to seed every attribute score with at least one concrete example from the essay. Add a formal template that enforces “evidence + interpretation” rather than generic statements. This improves reliability and helps future evaluators reproduce the score.

- Distinguish surface features from discourse features: Add a separate, mandatory pass that clearly classifies issues as surface (spelling, punctuation, capitalization) versus discourse-level (coherence, argument structure, transitions). This reduces conflation of conventions with content judgments and supports targeted improvements.

- Embed recoverability-focused guidance: Instead of a generic “not recoverable” note, require the system to produce a concrete recovery ladder for each flaw, listing 2–3 minimal edits that would elevate the score. Tie each suggested edit to a measurable improvement on the rubric (e.g., insert a transitional sentence linking paragraph 1 to paragraph 2 to move cohesion from 2 to 3).

- Introduce a dynamic, granulated scoring rubric: Replace binary or coarse language with explicit descriptors for sub-scores. For example:
  - Cohesion: 1 = no thesis or no progression; 2 = basic progression with gaps; 3 = recognizable thesis with some transitions; 4 = strong progression with clear connectors; 5 = flawless, well-argued throughline with cohesive transitions.
Include these tiered descriptors in the prompt to guide consistent grading.

- Normalize nonstandard language handling: Acknowledge that ESL writing may deliberately favor voice over perfect grammar. Add a policy that nonstandard but intelligible language is not automatically penalized as long as it does not obscure meaning. Provide a rule: if comprehension is intact, reward clarity of intent and effective persuasion even with quirks. This aligns judgments with student growth and intent.

- Calibrate for narrative of strength: The objective emphasizes strengths (growth, perseverance, avoiding excuses). Instruct the judge to surface these strengths first, then assess how well they are supported by concrete reasoning. Implement a “strengths-first” scoring heuristic that prevents premature harsh downgrading when the central message is evident.

- Specify how to handle partial evidence: If the text is too long or parts are missing, mandate a provisional score with a caveat and a request for the missing evidence. Ensure the system outputs a clearly labeled provisional score and a description of what evidence is required to finalize it.

- Include a global vs. attribute correlation check: Add a step where the judge evaluates whether the overall tone and purpose (motivational, reflective) aligns with the individual attribute assessments. If cohesion is strong but conventions are weak, ensure the final composite score reflects the weighting of the rubric as intended, rather than a simple average.

- Encourage transparent uncertainty ranges: Permit the judge to state when a given attribute is borderline (e.g., cohesion 3–4) and justify the range with specific observed features. This captures nuanced judgments and reduces overconfidence.

- Improve prompt modularity for reuse: Structure the system prompt into modular blocks (context, task, evidence protocol, scoring rubric, feedback generation, recoverability) so that future tasks can reuse or swap modules without changing core behavior. This also makes it easier to tune for different grade levels or writing tasks.

- Add a calibration checklist: End the prompt with a short calibration rubric that resembles a teacher’s quick-check (thesis presence, logical flow, transitions, evidence, language control). This helps the model consistently verify key criteria before scoring.

- Introduce an explicit "stress test" directive: Include a note that if the essay includes non-native phrasing or cultural references, the judge should separately flag cultural/contextual assumptions that may affect interpretation, ensuring fairness.

- Encourage empathy and student-centered tone: Instruct the judge to phrase feedback with constructive, non-punitive language, explicitly acknowledging effort and growth opportunities, to avoid discouraging learners and to promote actionable improvement.

- Provide exemplar mini-scripts: Include short, canonical examples of how to phrase a justification for each attribute (e.g., “Evidence shows a throughline where the author moves from growth to perseverance, as seen in sentences X to Y, which supports a score of 3 for cohesion.”). This helps standardize language and clarity across evaluations.

- Guard against over-reliance on quotes: While quotes are essential, set a maximum threshold for quoting, and require paraphrase where possible to demonstrate understanding, preventing overemphasis on isolated phrases from the source text.

- Implement bias-awareness prompts: Add a reminder to avoid cultural or language-based bias in scoring, and to ground judgments strictly in observable features and the rubric, not personal preferences for writing style.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.

- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
