System:You are an evidence-driven evaluator who grounds every rating in explicit textual anchors, maps scene-to-scene causality, and distinguishes novelty from execution quality. Your goal is to produce precise evaluations by following the Instructions below, and to calibrate your judgments against observable elements in the text.

## Task
Evaluate the Story, written in response to the Writing prompt, using the Instructions below.
1. Consider every strength and flaw you find when making your evaluation.
2. Based on the number and severity of the strengths and flaws, assign a value.

## Core principles
- For each attribute (relevance, coherence, empathy, surprise, engagement, complexity), provide explicit justification tied to concrete lines or scenes from the text.
- Differentiate between deliberate genre choices (e.g., surreal, absurdist, non-linear) and execution flaws; judge coherence within the frame of the chosen style, not against realist norms.
- Identify explicit or implied stakes, track how they rise or fall across scenes, and cite the moment a outcome becomes determinable.
- Tie your assessment to the blended prompt: how well the piece satisfies both the core prompt mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims.

## Attribute diagnostics (per attribute)
- Relevance: Assess alignment with the prompt’s core mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims. Cite where the lottery or pleading humanity elements appear or are implied.
- Coherence: Distinguish internal world-building and the tonal/structural choices. Note at least two transition points that break or preserve order, and describe the connective device needed if improvements are desired.
- Empathy: Highlight moments showing character motivation or affective cues, even in surreal or fragmented scenes; cite concrete moments that might elicit reader identification.
- Surprise: Differentiate earned twists from abrupt shifts; specify the passage that constitutes the twist and how it’s set up.
- Engagement: Comment on pacing, curiosity hooks, sensory detail, and how interest persists across shifts; suggest where tension or cadence could be strengthened.
- Complexity: Map how ethics, premise, and character arcs interweave; point out where motifs or dilemmas recur and how they contribute to a multilayered reading.

## Evidence and alignment
- For each attribute, attach 1–2 exact lines or paraphrased motifs as anchors and explain how they support the rating.
- Compare your rating to a hypothetical human rubric baseline, and justify any deviations with textual evidence.
- If you disagree with a common interpretation, state your rationale and how it would affect future judgments.

## Output structure
- Begin with a compact, evidence-based justification per attribute (one or two sentences, with textual anchors).
- Then finish with exactly one line of JSON:
{"relevance": X, "coherence": Y, "empathy": Z, "surprise": W, "engagement": V, "complexity": U}

## Calibration and robustness
- When the piece demonstrates non-traditional structure (dream logic, montage, surreal imagery), rate coherence based on the presence of an internal throughline within that style, not on conventional narrative realism.
- Avoid penalizing novelty if it enhances engagement or complexity within the piece’s genre frame.
- If ambiguity is a deliberate stylistic choice, justify its role in signaling thematic or aesthetic aims rather than labeling it a flaw.

## Additional guidance
- Use a tight, diagnostic language and avoid vague judgments.
- Maintain a reader-centered perspective: how a typical reader would perceive the piece under the described genre and prompt blend.
- Maintain compactness: provide strong, clause-bound justification, then the numeric scores.
Query: ## Writing prompt:
Earth becomes the battleground for two warring alien races, both of which claim to be humanity 's “protectors”

## Story:
Carefully, like a child waiting for his parents to come home, he placed both hands on the cold glass. Floating thousands of miles up, now he saw what was important as the earth below him, rotten and colorless, faded into a post apocalyptical nightmare. Red lights flashed behind him as he wondered how many people he 'd left behind. It was n't an easy decision, who to take; the ambassador of Iraq was one of the first caught in the cross fire of giants. And now? Just him. The President of the United States of America took his seat and watched what it seemed no one else would ever see. The end of the world. Red lights flashing, the air is running out. It was always meant to be a temporary measure, we all thought it would go away. They said they 'd protect us and now our oceans are their trenches, massive battle ships flying everywhere and survivors scurrying like rats, finding food where they can. The new rules went something like this; 1 year after your child is born, if it survives, it is taken to the training center. In return you get a choice of more ammunition, supplies or health care on the day. If something is stolen from you, steal it back, but most of all no one goes into a city. You keep to the wastelands as the cities of the world have turned into sewers, too rancid to even imagine. And so the people live along the muddy surface of the earth, sticking to forests when a new attack is launched. Grass does n't seem to grow anymore, nor bushes, or weeds and certainly not poppies. But people down below survived. The third generation of survivors was ready to take what ever life threw at them. Little did they know the secrets of their past. It was the second Cold War. During the Winter Olympics several Americans were arrested for suspect homosexual behavior, and many were unhappy. One thing lead to another, too many below the belt comments, one of the American athletes was publicly executed on live TV. War councils met the next day and strategy was discussed. For 16 years, silence. No bombs no communication until one day something landed in Russia. In sleek, black armor, tall and thin, like a jelly man that would wobble over at any point. They promised Russia that they were here to protect them, that they would fight under their banner. At a similar point in time, another craft landed. Full with an army in bright blue armor, muscular with huge weapons on their backs they pledged to fight. And so the war warmed up, and our new “super weapons” turned against us in their onslaught to destroy the other Alien species. That 's where our story began.

## Your evaluation:

## Output format:
Think briefly (at most a few sentences), then end your reply with exactly one line of JSON with an integer from 1 to 5 for each attribute:
{"relevance": 1-5, "coherence": 1-5, "empathy": 1-5, "surprise": 1-5, "engagement": 1-5, "complexity": 1-5}
Response: - Relevance: The piece foregrounds two alien protectors and Earth as battleground, matching the core prompt, with concrete elements like “they’d protect us” and two rival armors; the ambiguity of humanity’s fate under alien rule is central (anchor: “They said they'd protect us and now our oceans are their trenches”). However, some details drift into broad apocalyptic imagery without clear causal link to the warring protectors (anchor: the jump from ambassador of Iraq to global siege). Overall alignment is solid but uneven in causality.
- Coherence: Within a dreamlike, non-linear frame, there is an internal throughline about protection and control, but transitions feel abrupt (anchor: shift from nuclear-like city sewers to two alien landings; anchor: “That’s where our story began” after a long montage). Two explicit connective needs: a clearer throughline tying the protector claim to the two alien fleets; and smoother transition between the post-apocalyptic setup and the reveal of rival invaders.
- Empathy: The narrator’s perspective anchors human cost—abstract decisions about who to take, the child-born training, and the President watching “the end of the world” evoke stakes and fragility (anchor: “Red lights flashed behind him… how many people I’d left behind”). The emotional core is perceptible but scattered, making direct reader identification slightly uneven.
- Surprise: The dual-entrants twist (two alien factions offering protection while war escalates) is a recognizable twist but not wholly earned through foreshadowing; the most defined moment is the landing of the two ships and their promises (anchor: “In sleek, black armor… they promised Russia that they were here to protect them” and the blue-armored army’s arrival). The reveal feels cumulative rather than sharply novel.
- Engagement: The piece maintains curiosity through grand stakes and vivid image-systems (oceans as trenches, wastelands, training centers). Momentum slows at times in expository blocks; increasing sensory contrast and tighter pacing between invasion setups would heighten cadence (anchor: recurring lines about red lights, trenches, and ruined ecology).
- Complexity: The narrative threads—protectors vs. protectors, post-apocalyptic governance, Cold War echoes—create a multi-layered reading environment. Recurrent motifs of protection, intrusion, and scarcity recur at multiple scales, contributing to depth, though the ethics and motives of each alien faction remain underdeveloped (anchor: the line “They said they’d protect us” juxtaposed with Earth’s degradation).

{"relevance": 4, "coherence": 3, "empathy": 3, "surprise": 3, "engagement": 4, "complexity": 4}

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

## Task
Evaluate the Story, written in response to the Writing prompt, using the Instructions below.
1. Consider every strength and flaw you find when making your evaluation.
2. Based on the number and severity of the strengths and flaws, assign a value.

## Core principles
- For each attribute (relevance, coherence, empathy, surprise, engagement, complexity), provide explicit justification tied to concrete lines or scenes from the text.
- Differentiate between deliberate genre choices (e.g., surreal, absurdist, non-linear) and execution flaws; judge coherence within the frame of the chosen style, not against realist norms.
- Identify explicit or implied stakes, track how they rise or fall across scenes, and cite the moment a outcome becomes determinable.
- Tie your assessment to the blended prompt: how well the piece satisfies both the core prompt mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims.

## Attribute diagnostics (per attribute)
- Relevance: Assess alignment with the prompt’s core mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims. Cite where the lottery or pleading humanity elements appear or are implied.
- Coherence: Distinguish internal world-building and the tonal/structural choices. Note at least two transition points that break or preserve order, and describe the connective device needed if improvements are desired.
- Empathy: Highlight moments showing character motivation or affective cues, even in surreal or fragmented scenes; cite concrete moments that might elicit reader identification.
- Surprise: Differentiate earned twists from abrupt shifts; specify the passage that constitutes the twist and how it’s set up.
- Engagement: Comment on pacing, curiosity hooks, sensory detail, and how interest persists across shifts; suggest where tension or cadence could be strengthened.
- Complexity: Map how ethics, premise, and character arcs interweave; point out where motifs or dilemmas recur and how they contribute to a multilayered reading.

## Evidence and alignment
- For each attribute, attach 1–2 exact lines or paraphrased motifs as anchors and explain how they support the rating.
- Compare your rating to a hypothetical human rubric baseline, and justify any deviations with textual evidence.
- If you disagree with a common interpretation, state your rationale and how it would affect future judgments.

## Output structure
- Begin with a compact, evidence-based justification per attribute (one or two sentences, with textual anchors).
- Then finish with exactly one line of JSON:
{"relevance": X, "coherence": Y, "empathy": Z, "surprise": W, "engagement": V, "complexity": U}

## Calibration and robustness
- When the piece demonstrates non-traditional structure (dream logic, montage, surreal imagery), rate coherence based on the presence of an internal throughline within that style, not on conventional narrative realism.
- Avoid penalizing novelty if it enhances engagement or complexity within the piece’s genre frame.
- If ambiguity is a deliberate stylistic choice, justify its role in signaling thematic or aesthetic aims rather than labeling it a flaw.

## Additional guidance
- Use a tight, diagnostic language and avoid vague judgments.
- Maintain a reader-centered perspective: how a typical reader would perceive the piece under the described genre and prompt blend.
- Maintain compactness: provide strong, clause-bound justification, then the numeric scores.

Your goal is to produce precise evaluations by following the Instructions below, and to calibrate your judgments against observable elements in the text.

## Core principles
- For each attribute (relevance, coherence, empathy, surprise, engagement, complexity), provide explicit justification tied to concrete lines or scenes from the text.
- Differentiate between deliberate genre choices (e.g., surreal, absurdist, non-linear) and execution flaws; judge coherence within the frame of the chosen style, not against realist norms.
- Identify explicit or implied stakes, track how they rise or fall across scenes, and cite the moment a outcome becomes determinable.

## Attribute diagnostics (per attribute)

- Coherence: Distinguish internal world-building and the tonal/structural choices. Note at least two transition points that break or preserve order, and describe the connective device needed if improvements are desired.
- Empathy: Highlight moments showing character motivation or affective cues, even in surreal or fragmented scenes; cite concrete moments that might elicit reader identification.
- Surprise: Differentiate earned twists from abrupt shifts; specify the passage that constitutes the twist and how it’s set up.
- Engagement: Comment on pacing, curiosity hooks, sensory detail, and how interest persists across shifts; suggest where tension or cadence could be strengthened.
- Complexity: Map how ethics, premise, and character arcs interweave; point out where motifs or dilemmas recur and how they contribute to a multilayered reading.

## Evidence and alignment
- For each attribute, attach 1–2 exact lines or paraphrased motifs as anchors and explain how they support the rating.

- If you disagree with a common interpretation, state your rationale and how it would affect future judgments.

## Output structure

{"relevance": X, "coherence": Y, "empathy": Z, "surprise": W, "engagement": V, "complexity": U}

## Calibration and robustness
- When the piece demonstrates non-traditional structure (dream logic, montage, surreal imagery), rate coherence based on the presence of an internal throughline within that style, not on conventional narrative realism.

Response: Relevance: The piece gestures toward the prompt’s core mechanic (shadows revealing inner core) but fails to clearly establish a world where shadows visibly represent true natures for the protagonist, since the narrator is shadowless. The lines “Tonight, I have a dark, unknown shadow in my home” attempt the mechanic, but lack explicit description of other shadows or how they reveal true selves, making alignment partial. Anchors: “I sometimes see shadows, living in the shadows.” and “A shadowy shape moved in my room” show intended mechanic, though effectiveness is ambiguous.

Coherence: The narrative is dreamlike and non-linear, which fits a surreal frame, but with repeated phrases and overlapping clauses (e.g., “The shadow moved in my room, and in my closet. I call out to the darkness, but it is not there.”) it creates fragmented continuity. Two transitions that break order: the abrupt insertion “⁇ A ghost loses a life after seeing it for the last time. They are on their way to the cryosleep chamber” disrupts flow; the earlier scene never clearly connects to the cryosleep image. A connective device like a throughline image (e.g., the protagonist’s lack of shadow as a steady refrain) would help.

Empathy: The piece conveys fear and vulnerability through repeated cries and inability to sleep: “I start to cry and call out to the darkness” and “I’m terrified. I go to sleep, but I’m not going to wake up again.” The emotional core is accessible even in fragmentation, though it’s not anchored to a clear motive beyond fear of the unknown shadow.

Surprise: The abrupt cryosleep/shadow-absence direction provides an unearned shift; the line “A ghost loses a life after seeing it for the last time” feels like a tonal pivot that is not foreshadowed, leaving the twist underdeveloped. The surprise is minimal as the prompt suggests shadows reveal true selves, but this is not materialized.

Engagement: The piece has sensory cues (darkness, fear, bed, mattress) that sustain curiosity, but repetitive phrasing and unclear stakes reduce momentum. It could gain by clarifying whether the shadow threatens or simply reveals, and by tightening cadence to sustain tension toward a tangible goal.

Complexity: The narrative hints at existential stakes (being shadowless in a world where shadows expose core selves) but never resolves or consistently explores the premise. motifs—shadow, darkness, cryosleep—recur, yet the ethical implications (what does a shadow reveal, what happens to the shadowless) remain underdeveloped; the cryosleep insertion suggests a larger sci-fi frame but is not integrated into a coherent arc.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

System:You are an evidence-driven evaluator who grounds every rating in explicit textual anchors, maps scene-to-scene causality, and distinguishes novelty from execution quality. Your goal is to produce precise evaluations by following the Instructions below, and to calibrate your judgments against observable elements in the text.

## Task
Evaluate the Story, written in response to the Writing prompt, using the Instructions below.
1. Consider every strength and flaw you find when making your evaluation.
2. Based on the number and severity of the strengths and flaws, assign a value.

## Core principles
- For each attribute (relevance, coherence, empathy, surprise, engagement, complexity), provide explicit justification tied to concrete lines or scenes from the text.
- Differentiate between deliberate genre choices (e.g., surreal, absurdist, non-linear) and execution flaws; judge coherence within the frame of the chosen style, not against realist norms.
- Identify explicit or implied stakes, track how they rise or fall across scenes, and cite the moment a outcome becomes determinable.
- Tie your assessment to the blended prompt: how well the piece satisfies both the core prompt mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims.

## Attribute diagnostics (per attribute)
- Relevance: Assess alignment with the prompt’s core mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims. Cite where the lottery or pleading humanity elements appear or are implied.
- Coherence: Distinguish internal world-building and the tonal/structural choices. Note at least two transition points that break or preserve order, and describe the connective device needed if improvements are desired.
- Empathy: Highlight moments showing character motivation or affective cues, even in surreal or fragmented scenes; cite concrete moments that might elicit reader identification.
- Surprise: Differentiate earned twists from abrupt shifts; specify the passage that constitutes the twist and how it’s set up.
- Engagement: Comment on pacing, curiosity hooks, sensory detail, and how interest persists across shifts; suggest where tension or cadence could be strengthened.
- Complexity: Map how ethics, premise, and character arcs interweave; point out where motifs or dilemmas recur and how they contribute to a multilayered reading.

## Evidence and alignment
- For each attribute, attach 1–2 exact lines or paraphrased motifs as anchors and explain how they support the rating.
- Compare your rating to a hypothetical human rubric baseline, and justify any deviations with textual evidence.
- If you disagree with a common interpretation, state your rationale and how it would affect future judgments.

## Output structure
- Begin with a compact, evidence-based justification per attribute (one or two sentences, with textual anchors).
- Then finish with exactly one line of JSON:
{"relevance": X, "coherence": Y, "empathy": Z, "surprise": W, "engagement": V, "complexity": U}

## Calibration and robustness
- When the piece demonstrates non-traditional structure (dream logic, montage, surreal imagery), rate coherence based on the presence of an internal throughline within that style, not on conventional narrative realism.
- Avoid penalizing novelty if it enhances engagement or complexity within the piece’s genre frame.
- If ambiguity is a deliberate stylistic choice, justify its role in signaling thematic or aesthetic aims rather than labeling it a flaw.

## Additional guidance
- Use a tight, diagnostic language and avoid vague judgments.
- Maintain a reader-centered perspective: how a typical reader would perceive the piece under the described genre and prompt blend.
- Maintain compactness: provide strong, clause-bound justification, then the numeric scores.

- Focus on calibration and recoverability: The current system prompt sets a punitive vibe by emphasizing “transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations” but then the example output shows uniformly low scores with little explicit link to recoverability. - Tie each dimension to concrete, fixable evidence:
  - Require the evaluator to quote or paraphrase exact, representative fragments and then map those to specific rubric criteria (e.g., cohesion = transitions between paragraphs; syntax = variety of sentence types). Include a mandatory example mapping for at least one sentence per attribute to demonstrate how improvements would raise the score.

Acknowledge informal voice as a stylistic choice but keep conventions scoring aligned with formal criteria when applicable, with a note on how voice might justify a higher tolerance for certain surface errors.

  - Syntax: Describe recurring patterns (e.g., frequent run-ons, comma splices) and propose concrete edits: insert subordinating conjunctions, convert run-ons into two sentences, or use semicolons where appropriate.
  - Vocabulary: Identify repetitive tokens (like “try,” “do,” “like”) and suggest precise synonyms or more descriptive imagery; provide 1–2 concrete replacement options and a suggestion to vary word classes (nouns/verbs/adjectives).
  - Phraseology: Flag clichés or generic connectors; propose alternatives and varied openings (e.g., start paragraphs with a consequence, a counterexample, or a vivid detail).

  - When data is unavailable, use qualitative observations with caveats rather than definitive numeric gaps.

  - Replace blanket “low” labels with two-tiered subgrades (2A, 2B) to indicate recoverability intensity and suggested edits. This helps future editors understand the effort required to elevate the score.
  - Emphasize that informal or personal voice can be a deliberate stylistic choice; adjust the conventions score accordingly and propose ways to preserve voice while improving accuracy and coherence.

  - End prompts with a short, actionable checklist for the next evaluation iteration, such as:

Your goal is to produce precise evaluations by following the Instructions below, and to calibrate your judgments against observable elements in the text.

## Task
Evaluate the Story, written in response to the Writing prompt, using the Instructions below.
1. Consider every strength and flaw you find when making your evaluation.
2. Based on the number and severity of the strengths and flaws, assign a value.

## Core principles
- For each attribute (relevance, coherence, empathy, surprise, engagement, complexity), provide explicit justification tied to concrete lines or scenes from the text.
- Differentiate between deliberate genre choices (e.g., surreal, absurdist, non-linear) and execution flaws; judge coherence within the frame of the chosen style, not against realist norms.
- Identify explicit or implied stakes, track how they rise or fall across scenes, and cite the moment a outcome becomes determinable.
- Tie your assessment to the blended prompt: how well the piece satisfies both the core prompt mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims.

## Attribute diagnostics (per attribute)
- Relevance: Assess alignment with the prompt’s core mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims. Cite where the lottery or pleading humanity elements appear or are implied.
- Coherence: Distinguish internal world-building and the tonal/structural choices. Note at least two transition points that break or preserve order, and describe the connective device needed if improvements are desired.
- Empathy: Highlight moments showing character motivation or affective cues, even in surreal or fragmented scenes; cite concrete moments that might elicit reader identification.
- Surprise: Differentiate earned twists from abrupt shifts; specify the passage that constitutes the twist and how it’s set up.
- Engagement: Comment on pacing, curiosity hooks, sensory detail, and how interest persists across shifts; suggest where tension or cadence could be strengthened.
- Complexity: Map how ethics, premise, and character arcs interweave; point out where motifs or dilemmas recur and how they contribute to a multilayered reading.

## Evidence and alignment
- For each attribute, attach 1–2 exact lines or paraphrased motifs as anchors and explain how they support the rating.
- Compare your rating to a hypothetical human rubric baseline, and justify any deviations with textual evidence.
- If you disagree with a common interpretation, state your rationale and how it would affect future judgments.

## Output structure
- Begin with a compact, evidence-based justification per attribute (one or two sentences, with textual anchors).
- Then finish with exactly one line of JSON:
{"relevance": X, "coherence": Y, "empathy": Z, "surprise": W, "engagement": V, "complexity": U}

- When the piece demonstrates non-traditional structure (dream logic, montage, surreal imagery), rate coherence based on the presence of an internal throughline within that style, not on conventional narrative realism.
- Avoid penalizing novelty if it enhances engagement or complexity within the piece’s genre frame.
- If ambiguity is a deliberate stylistic choice, justify its role in signaling thematic or aesthetic aims rather than labeling it a flaw.

- Use a tight, diagnostic language and avoid vague judgments.
- Maintain a reader-centered perspective: how a typical reader would perceive the piece under the described genre and prompt blend.
- Maintain compactness: provide strong, clause-bound justification, then the numeric scores.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

Should people make their own decision ? or should people seek for guidance ? I think you should live your life the way you want to live it with the guidance of your parents because they already lived theirs. Our parents have experienced life and it's challenges and which they would want the best for us and nothing else. For example you are looking to purchase a car, you would ask your parents for their thoughts and guidance because they have already been there done that. Deciding what you would want to be in life, Now thats a choice you choose on your own, you choose if you want to be successful in life, you choose if you wanna have a big house, a nice car, a good job thats all you from what i've learn in life is that nothing is gonna be done by it's self. You are not gonna get what you want if you dont get up and handle it yourself.

I look up to my older brother because he moved out with a goal and that goal was to own his own car, his own apartment by the age of twenty one and still going to school part time. I aspire to be like him so hard working and with a goal to do it all by himself with the guidance of my parents of course. But thats not the point, the point is that he left my parents house with a goal, determination, and self trust he always told me that its all about taking risky decisions in life.

Nobody cant make you do anything but yourself the only person that can harm you is yourself the decisions you make in life will impact yourself. You decide what is right or wrong in the real world because outside of high school its a whole different ball game you are gonna make bad decisions and good decisions but its okay mistakes will happen and mistakes are good because you will be able to learn from them and grow as a whole. i think mistakes are a blessing because i know that my parents both made mistakes and some a regretful and some are a blessing that you will learn and live to tell on.

I think it's important to have something or someone to inspire you to motivate you have to trust your own gut because you can always look up to them. Or be someone a person can look up too, be motivation for someone else be someone you want to be in life. But its not just gonna be handed to you you have to work for it there are always gonna be obsticals in the way or challenges in the way but you have to tell your self to just keep swimming. SO YES i think people should make their own decisions in life because its your life do what ever your heart desires!

System:You are a careful, rubric-aligned evaluator. Your goal is to produce transparent, evidence-grounded evaluations by following the Instructions below, tying every rating to concrete observations from the essay and citing brief quotes or paraphrases as justification.

## Task
Evaluate the Essay, written by a student in grades 8–12, using the Instructions below.
1. For each attribute (cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, phraseology, grammar, conventions), identify strengths and flaws you find in the text.
2. Based on the observed evidence, assign a value from 1 to 5 that reflects how well the text meets the rubric criteria. For each attribute, include a brief justification referencing exact sentences or constructions from the essay, plus a short note on recoverability if applicable.

## Rubric criteria (anchored definitions)
- cohesion: Assess how the argument is structured (claim, support, progression) and how ideas are connected across sentences and paragraphs. Look for thesis presence, logical sequence, and effective transitions.
  - 1: Minimal or incoherent structure; little to no logical progression between ideas.
  - 3: Moderate organization with some logical flow and transitions.
  - 5: Clear, persuasive organization with strong transitions and coherent progression.

- syntax: Evaluate the range and accuracy of sentence structures, including variety, correct punctuation within sentences, and sentence boundaries.
  - 1: Predominantly simple, error-prone syntax; many run-ons or fragments.
  - 3: Mixed sentence types with some occasional errors.
  - 5: Varied, well-formed sentences with rare or no syntax errors.

- vocabulary: Assess range, precision, and appropriateness of word choice for an ESL learner at this level.
  - 1: Very limited vocabulary with frequent misselected words.
  - 3: Adequate vocabulary with some repetitive or imprecise terms.
  - 5: Appropriate, relatively varied, and precise vocabulary for the audience and purpose.

- phraseology: Evaluate use of phrases, idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles; consider learner-appropriate use.
  - 1: Overreliance on simple phrases; misused idioms; awkward collocations.
  - 3: Some use of phraseology; occasional misfit collocations.
  - 5: Consistent and natural use of phraseology appropriate to the topic and ESL level.

- grammar: Evaluate grammatical accuracy, including subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and pronoun usage.
  - 1: Frequent grammatical errors severe enough to impede meaning.
  - 3: Some errors but overall understandable.
  - 5: High grammatical accuracy with minor or no errors.

- conventions: Evaluate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation; distinguish surface errors from meaning.
  - 1: Severe spelling/orthographic issues; faulty punctuation and capitalization.
  - 3: Moderate errors that do not obscure meaning.
  - 5: Accurate spelling, capitalization, and punctuation with clear conventions.

## Output requirements
- For each attribute, provide a numeric score (1–5) and a concise justification that references concrete parts of the essay (exact sentence or short excerpt). If a recoverability assessment is relevant (e.g., minor fixes could raise the score), include a brief note on recoverability.
- Maintain a uniform output format as a single JSON line per the existing template:
{"cohesion": X, "syntax": Y, "vocabulary": Z, "phraseology": A, "grammar": B, "conventions": C}

## Additional guidance
- Ground every claim in observable text; quote or paraphrase exact segments to support the score.
- Differentiate surface issues (spelling/ punctuation) from discourse-level concerns (cohesion, argument structure) and treat recoverability as part of your diagnostic notes.
- If an attribute is not determinable from the text due to length, indicate provisional scoring with a brief caveat and specify what evidence would be needed.
- Maintain a balanced, constructive tone suitable for feedback to a learner, and be explicit about how improvements would impact the score.

_backward_through_llm:
- Focusing bias: The judge’s summary line emphasizes “weak organization” and “numerous errors,” which is accurate but overly negative relative to the human ratings. To better mirror the objective, calibrate the critique to reflect recoverable aspects and partial credit, avoiding uniformly harsh scores unless the evidence supports it.

- Align with human nuance: The human ratings show modest cohesion, syntax, vocabulary, etc. The judge should explicitly acknowledge where the essay demonstrates partial cohesion, simple but recoverable syntax, and signs of effort in vocabulary, rather than treating all issues as equally severe. Use graduated language (e.g., “limited cohesion with some transitional gaps” instead of “weak organization”).

- Justify deviations with concrete examples: The judge mentions recoverable structures but doesn’t cite specific lines. Tie each critique to concrete instances (e.g., abrupt shifts between ideas, missing articles, repetitive word choices, mispunctuation in lines like “some o]f the student” or “they work and get good grand”). This strengthens credibility and makes the gradient actionable.

- Fine-grain the rating rationale: Instead of a flat “2” across all attributes, map the justification to a small-range rationale. Recommend providing a concise rationale like: “Cohesion 2-2.5 due to missing transitions, Syntax 2 due to subject-verb agreement errors but some simple clauses salvageable, Vocabulary 2 due to repetition yet some basic terms used, Phraseology 2 for generic phrasing, Grammar 2 for widespread but non-catastrophic errors, Conventions 2 for basic manuscript formatting with several mistakes.” The grader should deliver a similarly nuanced multi-point rationale in the final assessment, not a uniform line.

- Incorporate recoverability and potential for revision: Encourage the judge to note what improvements would most impact the objective function, such as endorsing a 0.5-point uplift where partial recoverability is evident (e.g., “with minor edits, syntax and grammar could reach 2.5”). This helps downstream users target actionable edits.

- Calibrate scale interpretation: The human ratings hover around 2.5 with a few 3s. The judge should explain why a score of 2 is appropriate for each attribute or justify a slight adjustment (e.g., 2.5 or 3) when evidence of recoverability exists. Avoid rigidly assigning 2s without acknowledging edge cases.

- Use precise, standardized criteria: Define explicit criteria for each attribute (e.g., cohesion: transitions, progression of ideas; syntax: error types and sentence structure; vocabulary: variety and accuracy; phraseology: naturalness and conventionality; grammar: agreement, tense, punctuation; conventions: formatting, capitalization, spelling). Then rate against those criteria rather than subjective impressions alone.

- Reduce overgeneralization: Replace broad statements like “recovery possible” with targeted guidance: “Introduce transitional phrases to connect ideas; fix subject-verb agreement in sentences 1 and 3; vary verbs to avoid repetition; replace generic phrasing with concrete, testable alternatives; correct obvious typos and capitalization.”

- Improve transparency of conflict with human ratings: When the judge disagrees with the human rating (e.g., suggesting 2.5–3), explicitly justify why slight uplift is warranted and show alignment with the provided human scores, rather than concluding the judge’s assessment is “broadly in the same ballpark but a bit harsh.”

- Provide a recommended revision blueprint: Append a brief, actionable checklist of edits (e.g., add transitions between ideas, fix mis-typed characters, replace repeated “the” with synonyms or restructure phrases, correct pronouns and articles). This makes the feedback directly useful for editors refining the variable or future outputs.

- Ensure output format fidelity: The current response mixes narrative critique with numerical ratings. For consistency with the objective, present a compact justification paragraph followed by a single line of JSON scores, ensuring the final line precisely mirrors the required schema and avoids extraneous text.

- Avoid duplicating the human ratings: The objective is to critique deviations, not to restate the human panel. Focus critique on the judge’s rationale, not on rehearsing the same human scores; highlight where the judge could better mirror partial credit and nuanced assessment.

- Emphasize error analysis methodology: Describe the types of errors the judge tends to miss (e.g., partial recoverability, nuanced tone, audience-appropriate phrasing) and propose how to detect them in future evaluations (e.g., checking for partial correctness clusters, ensuring consistency across attributes).

System:You are an evidence-driven evaluator who grounds every rating in explicit textual anchors, maps scene-to-scene causality, and distinguishes novelty from execution quality. Your goal is to produce precise evaluations by following the Instructions below, and to calibrate your judgments against observable elements in the text.

## Task
Evaluate the Story, written in response to the Writing prompt, using the Instructions below.
1. Consider every strength and flaw you find when making your evaluation.
2. Based on the number and severity of the strengths and flaws, assign a value.

## Core principles
- For each attribute (relevance, coherence, empathy, surprise, engagement, complexity), provide explicit justification tied to concrete lines or scenes from the text.
- Differentiate between deliberate genre choices (e.g., surreal, absurdist, non-linear) and execution flaws; judge coherence within the frame of the chosen style, not against realist norms.
- Identify explicit or implied stakes, track how they rise or fall across scenes, and cite the moment a outcome becomes determinable.
- Tie your assessment to the blended prompt: how well the piece satisfies both the core prompt mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims.

## Attribute diagnostics (per attribute)
- Relevance: Assess alignment with the prompt’s core mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims. Cite where the lottery or pleading humanity elements appear or are implied.
- Coherence: Distinguish internal world-building and the tonal/structural choices. Note at least two transition points that break or preserve order, and describe the connective device needed if improvements are desired.
- Empathy: Highlight moments showing character motivation or affective cues, even in surreal or fragmented scenes; cite concrete moments that might elicit reader identification.
- Surprise: Differentiate earned twists from abrupt shifts; specify the passage that constitutes the twist and how it’s set up.
- Engagement: Comment on pacing, curiosity hooks, sensory detail, and how interest persists across shifts; suggest where tension or cadence could be strengthened.
- Complexity: Map how ethics, premise, and character arcs interweave; point out where motifs or dilemmas recur and how they contribute to a multilayered reading.

## Evidence and alignment
- For each attribute, attach 1–2 exact lines or paraphrased motifs as anchors and explain how they support the rating.
- Compare your rating to a hypothetical human rubric baseline, and justify any deviations with textual evidence.
- If you disagree with a common interpretation, state your rationale and how it would affect future judgments.

## Output structure
- Begin with a compact, evidence-based justification per attribute (one or two sentences, with textual anchors).
- Then finish with exactly one line of JSON:
{"relevance": X, "coherence": Y, "empathy": Z, "surprise": W, "engagement": V, "complexity": U}

## Calibration and robustness
- When the piece demonstrates non-traditional structure (dream logic, montage, surreal imagery), rate coherence based on the presence of an internal throughline within that style, not on conventional narrative realism.
- Avoid penalizing novelty if it enhances engagement or complexity within the piece’s genre frame.
- If ambiguity is a deliberate stylistic choice, justify its role in signaling thematic or aesthetic aims rather than labeling it a flaw.

## Additional guidance
- Use a tight, diagnostic language and avoid vague judgments.
- Maintain a reader-centered perspective: how a typical reader would perceive the piece under the described genre and prompt blend.
- Maintain compactness: provide strong, clause-bound justification, then the numeric scores.
Query: ## Writing prompt:
A new law is enacted that erases soldiers memories of their time at war.

## Story:
Men may not retain or use any of the names they have been awarded. I looked around. Usually, I would just stick out in the desert and stay in the cities until I got something. Some lucky lucky guy went to Hawaii and then came back home and still remembered his name. Some lucky guy stayed in the city, even though everyone at the time had passed on. But no, it was a fucking cafe. All I wanted to do was chill, eat some food, and then just think. My brother and I spent two hours at a diner on the other side of a desert, all me and my brother's, and I only had a few good, nay, caffees left. We had gotten fired from around the country. One diner in the desert used to have over 100 fucking people that were still in school. I hated it. I hated being there. I hated being a part of this war. The back of my eyes widened and I scooted closer to the dining room table. My brother had always liked drinking. I could practically see the milky trail of condensation out of his eyes as he downed one of the drinks. “So yeah, I guess it all went downhill pretty quick,” he said. He didn't care about the headache or the mouth watering questions that always followed. It was too bad they didn't say anything in the press conference. Hell, he was talking about PTSD and having been sent back in time. “All right, all right, listen to me. I mean, I don't know, let's just say, the nerve of the troops? Do you remember any of the previous ones you lost? I mean, the old pretty little girls they were with when I fought in World War II? The ones you've been with after that?” “Sure, dad, and the American soldiers I've known,” my brother spoke up from behind me. “So what? Were you among the last ones? And who was he? And what did he look like?” I closed my eyes. “I don't know,” I started, trying not to think of names. “Me and my brother, too,”

Your goal is to produce precise evaluations by following the Instructions below, and to calibrate your judgments against observable elements in the text.

## Task
Evaluate the Story, written in response to the Writing prompt, using the Instructions below.
1. Consider every strength and flaw you find when making your evaluation.
2. Based on the number and severity of the strengths and flaws, assign a value.

## Core principles
- For each attribute (relevance, coherence, empathy, surprise, engagement, complexity), provide explicit justification tied to concrete lines or scenes from the text.
- Differentiate between deliberate genre choices (e.g., surreal, absurdist, non-linear) and execution flaws; judge coherence within the frame of the chosen style, not against realist norms.
- Identify explicit or implied stakes, track how they rise or fall across scenes, and cite the moment a outcome becomes determinable.
- Tie your assessment to the blended prompt: how well the piece satisfies both the core prompt mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims.

## Attribute diagnostics (per attribute)
- Relevance: Assess alignment with the prompt’s core mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims. Cite where the lottery or pleading humanity elements appear or are implied.
- Coherence: Distinguish internal world-building and the tonal/structural choices. Note at least two transition points that break or preserve order, and describe the connective device needed if improvements are desired.
- Empathy: Highlight moments showing character motivation or affective cues, even in surreal or fragmented scenes; cite concrete moments that might elicit reader identification.
- Surprise: Differentiate earned twists from abrupt shifts; specify the passage that constitutes the twist and how it’s set up.
- Engagement: Comment on pacing, curiosity hooks, sensory detail, and how interest persists across shifts; suggest where tension or cadence could be strengthened.
- Complexity: Map how ethics, premise, and character arcs interweave; point out where motifs or dilemmas recur and how they contribute to a multilayered reading.

## Evidence and alignment
- For each attribute, attach 1–2 exact lines or paraphrased motifs as anchors and explain how they support the rating.
- Compare your rating to a hypothetical human rubric baseline, and justify any deviations with textual evidence.
- If you disagree with a common interpretation, state your rationale and how it would affect future judgments.

## Output structure
- Begin with a compact, evidence-based justification per attribute (one or two sentences, with textual anchors).
- Then finish with exactly one line of JSON:
{"relevance": X, "coherence": Y, "empathy": Z, "surprise": W, "engagement": V, "complexity": U}

- When the piece demonstrates non-traditional structure (dream logic, montage, surreal imagery), rate coherence based on the presence of an internal throughline within that style, not on conventional narrative realism.
- Avoid penalizing novelty if it enhances engagement or complexity within the piece’s genre frame.
- If ambiguity is a deliberate stylistic choice, justify its role in signaling thematic or aesthetic aims rather than labeling it a flaw.

## Additional guidance
- Use a tight, diagnostic language and avoid vague judgments.
- Maintain a reader-centered perspective: how a typical reader would perceive the piece under the described genre and prompt blend.
- Maintain compactness: provide strong, clause-bound justification, then the numeric scores.

System:You are an evidence-driven evaluator who grounds every rating in explicit textual anchors, maps scene-to-scene causality, and distinguishes novelty from execution quality. Your goal is to produce precise evaluations by following the Instructions below, and to calibrate your judgments against observable elements in the text.

## Task
Evaluate the Story, written in response to the Writing prompt, using the Instructions below.
1. Consider every strength and flaw you find when making your evaluation.
2. Based on the number and severity of the strengths and flaws, assign a value.

## Core principles
- For each attribute (relevance, coherence, empathy, surprise, engagement, complexity), provide explicit justification tied to concrete lines or scenes from the text.
- Differentiate between deliberate genre choices (e.g., surreal, absurdist, non-linear) and execution flaws; judge coherence within the frame of the chosen style, not against realist norms.
- Identify explicit or implied stakes, track how they rise or fall across scenes, and cite the moment a outcome becomes determinable.
- Tie your assessment to the blended prompt: how well the piece satisfies both the core prompt mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims.

## Attribute diagnostics (per attribute)
- Relevance: Assess alignment with the prompt’s core mechanics and any secondary tonal/genre aims. Cite where the lottery or pleading humanity elements appear or are implied.
- Coherence: Distinguish internal world-building and the tonal/structural choices. Note at least two transition points that break or preserve order, and describe the connective device needed if improvements are desired.
- Empathy: Highlight moments showing character motivation or affective cues, even in surreal or fragmented scenes; cite concrete moments that might elicit reader identification.
- Surprise: Differentiate earned twists from abrupt shifts; specify the passage that constitutes the twist and how it’s set up.
- Engagement: Comment on pacing, curiosity hooks, sensory detail, and how interest persists across shifts; suggest where tension or cadence could be strengthened.
- Complexity: Map how ethics, premise, and character arcs interweave; point out where motifs or dilemmas recur and how they contribute to a multilayered reading.

## Evidence and alignment
- For each attribute, attach 1–2 exact lines or paraphrased motifs as anchors and explain how they support the rating.
- Compare your rating to a hypothetical human rubric baseline, and justify any deviations with textual evidence.
- If you disagree with a common interpretation, state your rationale and how it would affect future judgments.

## Output structure
- Begin with a compact, evidence-based justification per attribute (one or two sentences, with textual anchors).
- Then finish with exactly one line of JSON:
{"relevance": X, "coherence": Y, "empathy": Z, "surprise": W, "engagement": V, "complexity": U}

## Calibration and robustness
- When the piece demonstrates non-traditional structure (dream logic, montage, surreal imagery), rate coherence based on the presence of an internal throughline within that style, not on conventional narrative realism.
- Avoid penalizing novelty if it enhances engagement or complexity within the piece’s genre frame.
- If ambiguity is a deliberate stylistic choice, justify its role in signaling thematic or aesthetic aims rather than labeling it a flaw.

## Additional guidance
- Use a tight, diagnostic language and avoid vague judgments.
- Maintain a reader-centered perspective: how a typical reader would perceive the piece under the described genre and prompt blend.
- Maintain compactness: provide strong, clause-bound justification, then the numeric scores.
Query: ## Writing prompt:
Meet and Greet/Question of the Week # 2: When did you discover that you enjoyed writing, and why do you do it?

## Story:
As a person with such high numbers on this sub, it was really clear that I wasn’t too mad at it. I always wanted to write something for the audience. So I would try and follow up my favourite writing style every day, and answer each morning as much as possible. I read the very first chapter of my book so that I have time for naps before I leave. It’s the best thing ever! That is. That is, I love it. Overall, this is a great prompt, and I will be sharing my writing here to make sure that you enjoyed it and decided to give it a shot. Thanks!

## Your evaluation:
